newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia Airlines sees $5 mln net in 96 vs 95 loss.
newsitem.headline: Croatia Airlines sees $5 mln net in 96 vs 95 loss.

text.p: Croatian flag carrier Croatia Airlines said on Monday it expected a net profit in the region of $5 million for 1996, compared to a $3.44 million 1995 loss.
"Almost all targets were fullfilled and in most segments plans were overshot," it said in a preliminary profit statement faxed to Reuters.
The company revamped its marketing and sales strategies and imposed stronger controls on costs and investment, while also rationalising employment, it said.
Croatia did not say whether it actually made any job cuts.
"In this way the 1995 loss...was completely covered and capital erosion prevented, improving the company's business credibility," the statement added.
This was seen as helping to secure fresh financial support from banks for the airline's amibitious expansion plans.
Benefitting from a 21.5-percent increase in passenger traffic and more cargo, its total 1996 revenue rose to around $114 million from $95.3 million a year earlier.

Operating profit was put at roughly $14 million, with costs and debt servicing swallowing $9 million. Some of the annuities for the purchase of the original nine-plane fleet cease at the end of this year.
But Croatia Airlines will have to raise new loans to pay for six Airbus medium-range A319 aircraft, ordered for delivery between 1998 and 2000.
The 1996 preliminary figures showed regular passengers at 823,000, overshooting the target by three percent. Passenger load factor (PLF) was boosted to 58 from 50.2 percent.
Croatia also carried 96,000 charter passengers and 4,745 tonnes of cargo and mail, three percent more than in 1995.

The government made an initial step toward fully privatising the airline by offering its 27.10-percent stake, valued at just under $14 million, for vouchers under a mass privatisation scheme later this year.

Among its shareholders are Zagreb Airport with 14.2 percent and the state privatisation agency with another 9.5 percent. Private individuals have around eight percent in it and a number of Croatian firms with smaller stakes control the rest. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
